The seasons on Earth are caused by the planet's axial tilt of approximately 23.5 degrees as it orbits the Sun. Because of this tilt, different parts of the Earth receive varying amounts of direct sunlight and experience different lengths of daylight throughout the year. When a hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it receives more concentrated solar energy and longer days, resulting in summer; conversely, when a hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, it receives less direct sunlight and shorter days, resulting in winter. The transitional seasons of spring and autumn occur when neither hemisphere is tilted significantly toward or away from the Sun.
